title: The reference library predicts a new run, and a larger model is checked against it
design_ref: Building intuition: the reference result library; check at one larger scale
purpose: Use the sweep's table the way the design intends: ask it what a setting should do, run that setting with a seed it has not seen, and compare. Then repeat two cells of the grid on a model nearly three times larger to see whether the small-scale pattern holds.

steps.output:
lr 3e-6, K=8: expected held-out pass rate 0.537 (best seen 0.548, the two seeds differ by 0.051, behavior KL 0.0016, ESS 0.997)
lr 3e-6, K=16: expected held-out pass rate 0.502 (best seen 0.507, the two seeds differ by 0.007, behavior KL 0.0025, ESS 0.995)

steps.display: python reference_lookup.py --lr 1e-5 --correction decoupled --staleness 1 8   # a setting the library has a warning for
steps.output:
lr 1e-5, K=1: expected held-out pass rate 0.302 (best seen 0.469, the two seeds differ by 0.141, behavior KL 0.0006, ESS 0.999)  WARNING: 2 of 2 runs at this setting collapsed
lr 1e-5, K=8: expected held-out pass rate 0.477 (best seen 0.492, the two seeds differ by 0.031, behavior KL 0.0106, ESS 0.971)

steps.display: # sweep library-check-s09: 2 cells read back from the state bucket (already complete)
python compare_with_library.py library-check-s09   # a seed the sweep did not use
steps.output:
K=8: library said 0.537, new run (seed 3) got 0.569, difference +0.032
K=16: library said 0.502, new run (seed 3) got 0.490, difference -0.012

steps.display: # sweep larger-scale-s09: 2 cells read back from the state bucket (already complete)
python larger_scale.py larger-scale-s09   # the same two cells of the grid, on Qwen3-1.7B (0.6B in the sweep)

checks.description: both library lookups were answered from the sweep's table
checks.because: The table is the sweep's output stored with the recipe, so 'can I set staleness to 8?' has an answer that does not require a new run.

checks.description: the library flags the setting that is unstable: at the larger learning rate with no staleness both runs collapsed, and the answer says so
checks.because: 'Can I set staleness to 1 at this learning rate?' has the answer 'not reliably, and staleness is not the reason' (S03). A table that gave a number without the collapse count would mislead.

checks.description: a new seed lands within the table's tolerance of the library's prediction at both settings (stable learning rate)
checks.because: The table averages two seeds; a third seed that falls within 0.06 of it (about twice the seed-to-seed spread seen in S03) shows the table predicts, rather than merely describes.

checks.description: on the larger model staleness still raises the behavior KL by at least ten times (K=16 against K=1)
checks.because: The mechanism does not depend on the model's size: more versions per batch means older samples and a larger gap to the target.

checks.description: on the larger model the behavior KL at K=16 is within a factor of ten of the small model's
checks.because: The design says to confirm two or three cells of the sweep on the target model before trusting the small-scale curve; here the confirmation is that the size of the gap carries over to within an order of magnitude.
Two cells on the 48 GB cards of the pool.

notes: What did not transfer: on the 0.6B model at this learning rate K=1 was the cell that collapsed (0.302) and K=16 held better (0.408). On the 1.7B model K=1 reached 0.580 and K=16 0.602: the larger model tolerates the rate with fresh data, and here the staleness is what costs. One seed each, so the size of the difference is uncertain; its direction is the opposite of the small model's. That is what the design's advice is for: the curve of the small model is a map of the mechanism, not of the target.
